articles.text: When the Silicon Valley Bank failed it sent shock waves through financial markets. Perhaps it shouldn’t have been a surprise that when discussing causation many Republicans attributed its collapse to the fact that it was a “woke” bank. What gave me pause was their use of the word “woke.” The word, initially regarded as slang, was added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2017, and is now a part of the mainstream language. It is derived from African-American vernacular, and was meant to describe one who is alert to and aware of the presence in society of prejudice and discrimination as well as systemic oppression and injustice. The term has since become contemporized. Beginning in 2014 it became identified with the Black Lives Matter movement and was often used during protests or when debating the role the police should play in society. But ultimately what does “woke” mean? Prior to its being appropriated by other activist groups, Perry Bacon, Jr., a columnist for the Washington Post, gave the term a comprehensive definition (one not necessarily shared by many centrist Democrats). He asserted that to be “woke” meant a rejection of American exceptionalism; incorporated the belief that America has never been a true democracy; that people of color suffer from systemic, institutional discrimination; that women suffer from inherent sexism; that individuals should be able to identify with any gender or even none; and that Donald Trump’s election was not an aberration, but a reflection of the prejudices regarding people of color held by a large part of the American population. “Woke” however, has recently been co-opted by conservatives and is often used as a single-word pejorative rallying cry when referring to progressives (or Democrats in general) and the issues they advocate. It is generally said with an insulting, denigrating sneer and is likely followed by the words “political correctness.” For example, Florida governor, Ron DeSantis – who will, presumably, soon announce his candidacy for president – in a recent speech characterized his state as “the place where ’woke’ goes to die”. Additionally he signed a law named “Stop the Woke Act.” We reject ‘woke’ ideology, he said, and “we will never surrender to the ‘woke’ agenda, or the ‘woke’ mob,” thus reminding his audience of his adherence to “anti-wokeness.” He has advocated the erasure of race-related content, the 1619 Project, African-American history courses in Florida’s high schools, and the Critical Race Theory. the definition of which is as elusive as the term “woke”. He has also supported barring transgender athletes from competing, and supported enhancing criminal penalties for people arrested for protesting during demonstrations (recall those that took place in reaction to the death of George Floyd). Our language is dynamic, ever changing, some words evolving into internet memes. Nouns (even proper nouns) can become verbs. An example would be the phrase, “I just bricked my phone,” meaning rendering it useless. Or. my sister “Houdinied her way out of a locked closet.” While some words seem to spontaneously appear in usage such as “woke”, others simply vanish. But for as long as they last, they are convenient shortcuts. Just ask any conservative whom you’ve “friended”. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Selen Ozturk Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) Sohrab “Seb” Ford (intern) Micah Temple (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: An incident at a high school basketball game at Piedmont High School on February 7 involving an adult male charged with battery on a male student appears to be unresolved by the school a month and a half later. Piedmont resident Yoel Asulin, was issued a 21-day Temporary Restraining Order by the Alameda County District Attorney’s office following the incident, and the order was extended for 21 more days this week. The victim, a high school senior, stated that he was grabbed violently in the bleachers and thrown down. His necklace was ripped and his shirt was torn. The student, who was emotionally distraught, was taken to a hospital and released. PHS Assistant Principal Erin Igoe, Athletic Director Bradley Smet, and Counselor Chris Hartford were on the scene, but did not call the police. The next day the boy, and four classmates who were with him at the game, gave their statements to the Piedmont Police. The incident did not appear on the Piedmont Police Department log. Since it was a late-reported event, the police did not file an emergency protective order. Police Capt. Chris Monahan confirmed that Asulin was charged with battery, which involves the act of physical harm, as opposed to assault, which also involves a threat of physical harm. Responding to a request for comments on March 7, Igoe said “While I was one of the school employees on scene, I don’t feel comfortable providing any comments. I will tell you, though, that choking is not what occurred.” Asulin has a prior arrest record. In 2015 he was arrested at his home for child endangerment under California Criminal Code 273A(A). On Tuesday, March 7, one month after the incident, PHS principal Sukanya Goswami sent an e-mail to PHS families about the incident. At that time she described as “a physical and verbal assault on one of our students at a varsity basketball game by a parent.” Goswami wrote, “A stay away letter has been issued to the adult involved. This stay away order means that this individual will not be allowed on campus for 14 days.” She added, “As a school system, we are re-evaluating the policies and procedures in place for communicating with students, parents and the greater community following any critical incident on campus.” However, neither the school nor the school district have yet specified when the stay-away letter was issued and whether it has been renewed, nor how the TRO will be enforced by the school district. articles.text: Scouting volunteers will be recognized at the Piedmont Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner on Thursday, March 30 in the guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. articles.text: More than 50 Piedmont community members gathered at Havens Library on Wednesday, March 15, to participate in a discussion with members of the Piedmont Police Department about community safety. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Captain Chris Monahan and other members of the police department led the discussion and participated in the event which provided a valuable discussion of the current social climate, preventive actions and community building. Bowers spoke about the diversity, equity, and inclusion training and initiatives by the police department, and highlighted the distinction between a hate crime and hate incident. “I am very appreciative of the opportunity to engage with the people who took the time out of their busy lives to hear from the Photos by Lisa Douglas Police Chief Jeremy Bowers spoke to community members about public safety on March 15 in the Havens library. Chief Jeremy Bowers (left), Mayor Jen Cavenaugh, PUSD’s DEI Director Dr. Vaanden Wyngard, Commander Lisa Douglas, PAAC Co-Presidents Cassindy Chao and Catherine Zhang, Black Youth Family Collective President Nairobi Kim, and Captain Chris Monahan. police department. It is clear that public safety continues to be one of the prime areas of focus for our Piedmont community,” said Bowers. “I look forward to the continued collaboration and conversations, because public safety is everyone’s responsibility,” he added. Monahan detailed some crime statistics, to include a spate of catalytic converter thefts. Monahan implored residents not to interfere with crimes-in-progress for their own safety. Converter thefts have been on the rise in Piedmont and throughout the Bay Area, and thieves at times are armed. Commander Lisa Douglas stressed the importance of not inundating 911 with non-emergency calls, and Sgt. George Tucker shared safety tips regarding property protection and lighting. Cassindy Chao and Catherine Zhang, co-presidents of Piedmont Asian Club, helped promote the meeting due to concerns of antiAsian hate and safety issues. “It is unfortunate in today’s society that people have been encouraged by politicians to be blatant in expressing anti-Asian hate expressions and crimes, anti-Semitism,” said Mary Geong of the Piedmont Asian American Club. The meeting included support by Black Youth Family Collective, Piedmont Jewish families, and the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. Nairobi Kim, President of the Black Youth Family Collective, said “Wednesday night was a wonderful representation of the community with Chief Bowers and his team at PPD. It warms my heart to see the many faces of our community come together.” For more information on community programs, crime statistics, and public safety tips, visit the Piedmont Police Department website at Piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/police.

articles.text: After a three-year absence due to Covid, the famed Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will return to Piedmont High School on Thursday, March 30, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. With the theme of “Maskarade,” guests are encouraged to show their creativity and wear bird=themed masks. Created in 1963, by PHS science teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck, the Bird Calling Contest grew into an annual event that over the decades has attracted national and international attention. The winners appeared for many years on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson, and then on Late Night with David Letterman. A panel of judges has been invited selected will consider the merits of the contestants based upon authenticity of call, poise and delivery, and content of contestants’ introduction of their bird. The judges include: • Rosemary Orozco, Weather forecaster KTVU • Michael Poryes, Television Producer. • Joe Fendel, 1991 Bird Calling Contest winner. • Jamie Mockel, PHS English teacher • Irma Munoz, PHS Vice Principal. Serving as celebrity judges will be Rosemary Orozco, a meteorologist at KTVU, and Michael Poryes, and 1982 PHS grad who created the popular television series “Hannah Montana.” Orozco taught at San Francisco State University and has worked as a meteorologist, journalist and news anchor for several stations. She also has worked as a model and has her own fashion line in San Francisco. Poryes is a three-time Emmy nominee who was an original member of the creative team that developed and launched “Saved by the Bell.” Joe Fendel was a four-time bird caller in 1987-91. First-year PHS English Teacher Jamieson Mockel comes from a family of bird callers, including his brother. His mother, Peggy, helped Leonard Wadeck with the show for many years. Assistant Principal, Irma Munoz is a former committee member for the Bird Calling Contest The contest will be directed by Piedmont High School Librarian Kathryn Levenson. “We have an able flock of student interns handling the technical aspects of the production. A student choreographed dance number will open the show and the student Jazz Quartet will entertain while the judged make their deliberations,” said Levenson. Tickets are available online at Showtix4u.com/event-details/67041. General admission tickets are $25; student tickets are $15. The Alan Harvey Theater is located at 800 Magnolia Avenue, on the high school campus. For more information contact Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@ piedmont.k12.ca.us, or 594-2781. articles.text: “Speak, Forgive, Forget,” echoed throughout Alan Harvey theater, as Piedmont High’s Advanced Acting class pushed the audience’s limits for forgiveness, with four dramatic performances of Everything is Wonderful the weekend of March 16-18. Written by Chelsea Marcantel, the play was directed by PHS Theater teacher Kimberly Taylor, with a talented rotating cast portraying an unlikely reunion of an Amish family. Junior Miranda Long, who has been acting since elementary school, carried the lead role of Miri in all four shows as the excommunicated daughter of an Amish couple intent on following their faith through forgiveness. “I really enjoyed playing Miri. I didn’t have to do an accent or wear the Amish dress for the whole play, but I appreciated how she was in an environment that was trying to encourage her just to forgive and forget.” When her brothers are killed in an accident, Miri returns to be with her family after being forced to leave five years earlier for not forgiving a man who assaulted her. Long continued, “Even though the high school usually doesn’t do such intense plays, I think it was important to spread awareness about the different struggles that the play highlighted, such Miranda Long (left) as the lead character Miri with Isabella Wire Eden Lorin (left) and Isabella Wire in traditional Amish dress Charles White (left), Miranda Long, Andres Roberts and Isabella Wire have a heated family discussion at a dinner table. as addiction, assault and grief. I appreciate that it brings to light those problems.” Senior Callan Mitchell, in his first performance as an actor, portrayed Jacob, the man who assaulted Miri. “It has been really weird performing such an upsetting character, and promoting the production, knowing that people might not view me the same,” said Mitchell, “It’s interesting to be myself one second in a classroom setting, and then go to rehearsal and play this terrible person.” Jake Hanke, a sophomore, took a major role in three performances as Eric, a young man struggling with alcoholism, who is taken in and forgiven by a couple whose sons he hit in a carand-buggy accident. “The play shows the importance of not having to forgive immediately, and giving yourself time to process your emotions,” said Hanke. Senior Charles White joined the acting class as a freshman. Despite COVID and having no theater on campus, he persisted in his acting pursuits to give his fourth and final Advanced Acting performance in Everything is Wonderful. He was cast as a stoic person with a beard in two performances as Miri’s father, Abram. “It is super unique what the acting class gets to do. We get to challenge ourselves as actors, especially with this play, while also being in a fun environment. Everyone is really good friends and we all had a great time,” said White. While the play encourages forgiveness, White acknowledged it’s not quite that simple. “The play has to do a lot with unconditional forgiveness, but also shows how not forgiving can be okay. People like to have a clean-cut resolution, where everybody is happy, but that doesn’t necessarily happen in this play,” White added.

articles.text: I am a focus coach in Piedmont and work with students and people with ADHD (Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder), helping them overcome obstacles and achieve their goals. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and my personal experience with ADHD to coach my clients. This week’s topic is Ego Depletion, one of the fundamental concepts I teach to clients who struggle with procrastination and completing tasks. Ego Depletion is the idea that each person only has a certain amount of self-control in a day and it depletes as it is used throughout the day. It’s that feeling of dread when you’re only halfway done with everything you need to do but your tank is empty and you have no energy left. The more willpower we use, the less we have… simple right? Some other things that deplete willpower besides using it are: stress, pain, multi-tasking, sleep deprivation, substances, a weak immune system, premenstrual cycle, and having low blood sugar. Now that we know that willpower is a set amount that depletes as we use it, how does that apply to ADHD and procrastination? People with ADHD often struggle to complete tasks from start to finish and frequently struggle with procrastination. I teach my clients about Ego Depletion as a way to get them to think strategically about how to prioritize their tasks. One exercise you can try is making a list of the things you need to do tomorrow and then ranking them in order of difficulty (make sure each task is broken down into one action item). List the willpower that you think you’ll need to get each one done. Once you have your list, you’re going to want to complete the tasks in order of how difficult they are and complete the most difficult ones first while you have the most willpower left. As you use up your willpower, you’ll have only the easy tasks to complete. Understanding and teaching ego depletion allows me to make effective to-do lists with my clients. Navigating a long to-do list can be very challenging for Strategize your to-do list. anyone, especially people with ADHD. Learning about ego depletion teaches people not only how to prioritize tasks, but also why it is so important to do the difficult tasks first. I use this and other concepts from Positive Psychology to teach and reinforce good habits so they can achieve their goals. What goals could you achieve if you knew the next steps? articles.text: Hedonists seek to maximize pleasure in life by indulging in anything and everything that elicits good feelings. To a hedonist, life is but a vehicle for happiness. Summer camps are not run by hedonists. If you handed a hedonist a summer camp, they would crumple at the sheer amount of displeasure that comes with the territory. Bugs. Dirt. Homesickness. Shared bathhouses. Surprise frogs in the showers of bathhouses. No amount of zip-lining could outdo the sacrifice of pleasure and comfort a hedonist craves. Yet, an untrained eye may believe Camp Augusta is engaging in this very act of folly: jamming so much unbridled fun into the day to somehow counteract the difficulties of rustic living. But that is not so. Watch and be amazed as we embrace displeasure at every turn. • Peer into the unflinching eyes of a counselor watching a camper notice the spider sharing their bunk. • Observe as the staff do absolutely nothing to install electricity or air conditioning into the cabins. • Be astounded when two campers who don’t get along are kept in the same cabin. Camp Augusta is not run by hedonists, oh no, no, no. Camp Augusta is run by people who understand that terribly arduous trials are in fact very healthy for children’s development. This isn’t to say we at Camp Augusta don’t also love fun and games (after all, we hire three Masters of Fun & Games to ensure maximum fun is to be had every season). We simply believe that a fun time and a challenging time can go hand in hand, and that challenge makes the summer camp experience sweeter (even if it isn’t felt in the moment). Those trials of terribly arduous displeasure mentioned earlier? Listen in for all to be revealed. • The spider lives at camp, too, and isn’t going to hurt us, so let’s figure out what to do together even if we feel a little scared of it. • Electricity and AC are great at home, but we can adapt to new situations even if they are uncomfortable at first. Let’s find a spot for your flashlight so you don’t need to scrounge for it later tonight… • I heard that you’re feeling really frustrated with another camper. I think we can still have a great week together and I’d love to know more about what’s going on and what you’re feeling. Behold! There is wonderful

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team continues its strong pace in the Western Alameda County Conference, beating Arroyo 3-1 at home on Wednesday, March 15, and shutting out Encinal 3-0 two days later on March 17, also in Binks Rawlings Gym. The pair of wins brings their record to 6-1 overall, notably including an Arroyo team with a lofty 12-3 record. “We actually had an off-day against Encinal. We had a starting outside hitter [John Champion] suffer an ankle injury right before the game, but we did fine,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. There’s a lot of energy around the team this season, now in its third year since reviving the program prior to the pandemic. With an arsenal of hitters and a vocal crowd in support, there is some swagger on the team that wasn’t present in previous seasons. “I think we’re playing a lot better this season because a lot of guys played club [volleyball] over the offseason,” said senior John MaNguyen, who led the team in kills against Encinal. “Last year we were a little more quiet and we weren’t really accustomed to playing together. This year, most of everyone played club, so we’ve gotten a lot better. We know how to work together because we’ve built close friendships. We try to keep the energy up every game and try to get in our opponents’ heads,” added senior Shunji Higashi, the team’s setter. With hitting options aplenty – MaNguyen, Wilson Wong, John Champion, and Torge Kraft, Higashi is able to send passes to either side comfortably to keep defenses off balance. “It’s really good to have options. When you’re limited to just one hitter, the other team will know and can prepare for it. You want variety,” said Higashi. 3-0 over Encinal It was a 3-0 sweep for the Highlanders against the Jets, winning by scores of 25-21, 25-16, and 25-19. In the first game, Encinal jumped out to a 2-0 lead, but PHS went on to score the next 10 of 11 points and never looked back. The two teams similarly traded points in the second game with Encinal briefly holding an 11-9 lead, but PHS then scored 10 of the next 12 points to lead 18-13, and then finished the second with five of the last six points. In the third game, PHS was able to rotate some bench players in and was still highly productive. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team improved its record to 6-2 with a pair of wins in the past week over Division 4 North Coast Section opponents. Playing in Vallejo on March 14, they defeated St. Patrick 9-2. Three days later, Saturday, March 18, they rolled past St. Helena 13-3 in a traditional early season game between the schools. It was an impressive pitching display for Piedmont with a juggled lineup. Infielder Peter Krumins tossed five innings and had 10 strikeouts against St. Helena, while Michael Aikawa,, also an infielder struck out eight in four innings against St. Patrick. “We don’t have a big roster and not a lot of pitchers. We’ll be a by-committee approach this season, but we have a great defense to back up our arms,” said coach Eric Olsen. 13-3 over St. Helena The Highlanders trailed 2-0 following the top of the third, but added runs in the bottom of the third and fourth innings to tie 2-2. The Saints went ahead 3-2 after the top of the fifth, but then Piedmont powered on nine runs in the bottom half to go clear ahead 11-3 and added two more runs in the bottom of the sixth to enact the 10-run rule. In the bottom of the fifth, Michael Aikawa led off with a walk and then sophomore centerfielder Markos Lagios stepped up to crack a two-run homer to centerfield to make it 4-3 Piedmont. With one out, Will Parker reached on a single and advanced to second on an error. Ryan McConathy then brought in Parker on a single, 5-3, followed by Dimitri Papahadjopolous drawing a walk. With John Olsen up, McConathy scored on a wild pitch, 6-3, followed by Papahadjopolous scoring on an error by the catcher, 7-4. From there, Piedmont drew walks from Liam Campbell and Aikawa—which brought in Olsen for another run, 8-3. Lagios then hit a two-run double to score Aikawa and Campbell, and then Peter Krumins hit a double to score Lagios for an 11-3 lead. In the bottom of the sixth, McConathy got things started with a walk followed by a single by Papahadjopolous. Olsen then hit a single to score McConathy, 12-3, then Campbell singled in Papahadjopolous to activate the 10-run rule at 13-3. articles.text: Long wins 800, Sorensen-Wald wins pole vault Piedmont’s track and field team competed in the Dublin Distance Fiesta on Friday and Saturday, March 17-18 and at the San Leandro Invitational at Burrell Field on March 18. At the Dublin Distance Fiesta, Parker Long won the 800 meters with a record time of 1:53.25. Pole vaulter Spencer Sorensen-Wald was first at the San Leandro Invitational with a personal record of 13 feet. Piedmont brought a combined 48 athletes to both events, with 41 athletes recording personal records. This year team has 90 athletes – the largest team in recent history. It was also a strong Dublin Distance for Christian Taylor, clocking a time of 4:18.67 in the 1600 meters to finish sixth out of a field of 1,147 runners. Coach Pouyan Assadi is hopeful Long and Taylor’s time will qualify them for the prestigious Stanford Invitational on March 31-April 1, and the Arcadia Invitational on April 7-8. “Parker and Christian take a lot of pride in being our captains,” said Assadi. “They constantly impress the coaching staff and are able to perform in the most intense environments. We’ve submitted their times to the Stanford and Arcadia invitationals and are waiting to hear back.” Long improved his previous best time by 10 seconds, winning his event against a field of 770 in Dublin. It marks the third fastest time in school history behind Gordon Johnson (1:51.10 in 1989), and Reece Proctor (1:52.64 in 2018). His time edged out Cooper Downing’s time of 1:53.40 set last year. “I’m still processing the aftermath of all of it just running that time. I got put in the fastest heat and I didn’t expect that to happen. Parker Long (17) won the prestigious Dublin Distance Fiesta’s 800 meter run in 1:53.25, notching the third fastest time in school history. The guy who got second [Justin Pretre] is committed to Cal and it was super intimidating going against a field like that. With 200 to go, I realized I might have the speed to win,” said Long. Long only competed in the 800 once last season and primarily raced the 1600 and 4x400 relay team. He was a key member of last year’s record-setting 4x400 alongside Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Parker Terrill. “I kind of avoided the 800 for a while, I focused on the mile and two-mile a bit more. After the first race of the season, my coach said I should consider focusing on the 800. In the 800, you have to be good at multiple things. The mile requires a lot of endurance and the 400 you can be good if you’re fast, but you need to have the speed and the endurance in the 800. I think I developed in both of those last year,” said Long. Sorensen-Wald’s height of 13-feet-0 was the best in a field of eight. It’s an impressive 2023 debut for Sorensen-Wald, whose previous best was 11 feet last year. The junior vaulter’s height at the San Leandro invitational ties him for third on the school’s all-time list with Irving Moore (1940), one foot behind No. 2 Marshall Wentworth (2011), and 3 feet, 1 inch behind Terrill’s alltime mark of 16 feet, 1 inch. “I was hoping to go higher in the pole vault, actually, practice has been going really well despite the rain holding us back a little. I didn’t jump in my sophomore year, so it took a bit to get back into it. Pole vaulting has a steep learning curve,” said SorensenWald about his development. It’s a similar start to the season as Piedmont’s record-setting pole vaulter Parker Terrill in 2022, who started his campaign last year with a vault of 13 feet, 1 inch at the Skyline Invitational. Like Terrill, Sorensen-Wald is hoping to develop in the decathlon. He also won the 300 meter hurdles in 42.41 in a field of 15 and tied for third in the 110 meter hurdles in 16.78. “Parker did every event and that’s something I’m trying to emulate. He did decathlon and was a great athlete, I’m trying to learn how to manage everything to not just put my complete focus on the pole vault but improve in other events as well,” said Sorensen-Wald. Spencer Sorensen-Wald cleared 13 feet in the pole vault at the San Leandro Invitational.

articles.text: The girls’ lacrosse team is back in action and has played five games. Piedmont’a girls’ lacrosse team is 2-3 through its first five matches of the season with a building team. They lost to Bishop O’Dowd 14-7 on Friday, March 17, but beat Cardinal Newman 12-6 on Wednesday, March 15. On March 14 they beat College Park 8-5, and lost 15-3 to Acalanes on March 7. Their season opened with a 17-5 loss to Miramonte on February 28. “We don’t have a superstar like in previous years, so they have to play together and for each other. Everything comes together,” said coach Carlton Chan. The Highlanders lost 10 players from the Class of 2022, including former leading scorer Katherine Kinne. Team leaders this year include Molly Ashton, Eleanor Lavin, Hailey Marshburn, and Lindsey Kottle. “Molly is our attack, and she’s been tremendous. She’s patent and she runs the offense. Eleanor is another captain; she is great in transition,” said Chan. Ashton has had a strong start to the season as the squad’s leading scorer with 15 goals including five against Bishop O’Dowd. “We are such underdogs, but we always work together. After the first couple of games, it feels like we’re getting things to work,” said Ashton. In its past two games, Piedmont has done well to stay composed, play good defense, and execute offensively. “When we understand what we need to do, we get it done. We have a team that works really well together,” said Ashton. 14-7 loss to Bishop O’Dowd The Dragons jumped out to an 8-2 lead in the first half, but Piedmont was able to score five second-half goals. Final stats: Ashton had five goals and one loose ball. Ruby Guzdar and Laurel Bentley scored once. Bentley also had three ground balls. 12-6 win vs. Cardinal Newman Piedmont went into halftime with a 4-4 tie but powered ahead with five consecutive goals in the second half to jump ahead 9-4 and finish with a 12-6 victory. articles.text: Piedmont Swim Team members and parents came together at the Piedmont Center for the Arts to hear from three high school seniors committing to swim in college next year, Simon Lins officially announced he’ll join the University of Virginia, Paige Arnold will swim at Amherst College in Massachusetts, and while Ryan Stokes will head to The College of Wooster in Ohio. “It’s been a pleasure to get to know them and their parents,” head coach Stefan Bill told a large crowd of friends and family members. The three Piedmont swimmers were joined on stage by their parents to share how they encouraged them to attend practice without being pushy. Amy Aubrecht, mother of Kate Aubrecht who started swimming for Amherst College, kicked off the discussion. “If there are any tricks. It was bribing with food, right? Like parents bringing hot chocolate or donuts,” said Aubrecht. Arnold agreed: “Every morning before morning practice, my dad gets up and makes my Ryan Stokes is set to join The College of Wooster in Ohio. Simon Lins officially announced he’ll join the University of Virginia. lunch, which is really nice, and he makes breakfast before early morning practices.” When these swimmers wanted to quit, this is how they pulled out of their slump. “In 6th grade I was fed up and dreading practice, but I had a conversation with my dad. He told me to give it one more year and if I still don’t like it, I can quit,” Lins told his Piedmont teammates. “The next year I fell in love with it.” Stokes added, “To just sit on the couch and miss practice, especially if you have a lot of schoolwork, is really easy. But for me, [it was] just telling myself you’ve gone this far, just one more practice.” Parents and swimmers agreed. The parents’ role in supporting their swimmer is simple. “Coaches coach, parents parent, swimmers swim,” Aubrecht explained. All of this support has given these kids the opportunity to swim in college. Simon is the first from Piedmont Swim Team in at least 10 years to be recruited by a Div. 1 school. “Every single school in the country with a D1 program was talking to me,” Simon admitted. “It was really overwhelming.” Simon was recruited by Cal, Harvard, University of Texas, Yale, Brown and Columbia to name a few but picked UVA. While his swim times were important, that wasn’t the only thing schools cared about. Paige Arnold will head to Amherst College in Massachusetts. “They are making an investment in you, not your times. They make an investment in your character and who you are striving to be,” Lins explained. Arnold committed to swim at Amherst College and Ryan at The College of Wooster. They say the process to swim at a Div. 3 school is different. While D1 schools recruit swimmers, for D3 schools are the ones who initiate it. Amy Aubrecht shared her daughter’s experience getting into Amherst. “You have to have the academics because there are no athletic scholarships,” she explained. College coaches have a certain number of swimmers they can support, which can help you get accepted into the school. Piedmont Swim Team head coach, Stefan Bil talked about his own conversations with college recruiters from around the country. “The Columbia men’s head coach essentially said, I’m going to put him [Lins} at the top of the list.” All the Piedmont swimmers say they sacrificed social events and the opportunity to play other sports. Parents gave up vacations to attend swim meets. “Every time I miss a practice, I think it’s a missed opportunity,” Arnold said. “When things get really hard it’s going to be discipline that will keep you consistent until motivation kicks in,” added Lins. Stokes summed it up: “Trust the process.”

articles.text: Former Music Director of San Francisco Symphony Michael Tilson Thomas comes out of retirement to conduct on March 30 to April 1. Michael Tilson Thomas returns from retirement to conduct the San Francisco Symphony Thursday through Saturday, March 30-April 1. Tilson Thomas, the revered long-time former music director of the Symphony, received 16 Grammy awards during his tenure; his first recording with the symphony, Prokofiev’s Romeo and Juliet, won a 1997 Grammy. He serves as Artistic Director Laureate of the New World Symphony, an American orchestral academy based in Miami Beach, Florida. Tilson Thomas will lead the symphony in three evening performances of the music of Gustav Mahler, for which he is well known. In London, Tilson Thomas led the London Symphony Orchestra in major festivals featuring the music of Steve Reich, George Gershwin, Johannes Brahms, and Mahler. Tilson Thomas’ discography includes The Mahler Project, a collection of the complete symphonies and works of Mahler for voice and orchestra performed with the San Francisco Symphony. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2022-23/MTT-Conducts-Mahler-6, or call the box office at (415) 864-6000. All performances begin at 7:30 p.m. ®

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory’s current production of Cambodian Rock Band continues through April 2. Lauren Yee’s rock-music themed play features songs by Dengue Fever, an American rock band based in Los Angeles that blends traditional Cambodian music with psychedelic rock. Yee’s play borrows tracks from the unique group to tell the story of a young Cambodian-American whose father was a musician persecuted by the Khmer Rouge army. The survivor returns to Cambodia for the first time in three decades, as his daughter prepares to prosecute one of Cambodia’s most infamous war criminals. Directed by Chay Yew, this darkly humorous play is set against a grim chapter of Cambodian history with live music by Dengue Fever. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www. berkeleyrep.org/shows/cambodian-rock-band/. Cambodian Rock Band is playing at Berkeley Repertory Theatre through April 2. articles.text: The de Young Museum is now exhibiting Lhola Amira: Facing the Future, a series of programs in an exhibition available throughout the year. The solo exhibition interprets the museum’s African art collection as a living and evolving practice through the lens of contemporary art. “Lhola Amira: Facing the Future” centers art from Africa as a site of critical exploration for the evolving nature of African culture. Lhola Amira, a South African artist, is offering visitors ways of becoming more open and more sensitized to the pain of others, and the possibilities of the present,” said Natasha Becker, curator of African art for the museum. Artworks from de Young’s permanent collection are placed with Amira’s work, exploring the themes of wounding and healing. Selections include African art pieces from the 19th and 20th century art, including sculptures and ceremonial pieces. On view is Philisa: Zinza Mphefumlo Wami (2022), an art portal considering sacred spaces for the cleansing of wounds, honoring ancestors, and fostering connection. Guests are invited to enter this interactive art portal with healing in mind. Also included in the exhibition is the single-channel video projection IRMANDADE: The Shape of Water in Pindorama (2018–2020), produced by Amira in Bahia, Brazil. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/lhola-amira. Installation of Lhola Amira: Facing the Future at the de Young Museum. articles.text: My professor taught a music course for non-majors and posed this very question, playing 3 or 4 recordings from concerts, each one fuzzier and less score-specific than the previous. I finally said no way to the last one, and now realize, years later, I was wrong. The 2022 winner of the Pulitzer Prize in Music, Raven Chacon, was inside the historic Mills College Concert Hall last week playing his own work entailing in part what he calls “noise music,” using an electric guitar. His music formerly would have been excluded because of a Pulitzer requirement that the music be written down and thus potentially replicated by others. There were no clear notes, nor bars nor rhythms nor chords nor tunes in the music, just sound – “noise.” Not even a visible score. This all-Chacon concert was the music of today, gaining great respectability, even better for watching than listening. Outside next to another campus building, a tireless young man with lacrosse stick was bouncing the ball off a wall in irregular patterns, with resonance. Was that also music? I’m not sure. But for Chacon, 45, and his audience, this was a historic time. Last year marked the first time in history that a Navajo Indian of the Indigenous People had ever won the muchsought-after Pulitzer in Music, which every composer-professor alive vies after. Among others. Chacon’s “Round” had six performers around a table activating electronics and a central turntable. There were roars, whooshes, and staticky sounds like shortwave radio still seeking a station. These seemingly semi-improvised sonic explorations reminded one of early electronic concerts in this very hall 50 or more years ago, going from loud to ultra-loud. Happily, free earplugs were there on a stand for the taking. Later, a solo for cello, “Quiver,” with growls, whirlwinds, bow scrapes and spiccato tones. In many ways, Ben Davis’ cello imitated electronic music for over 15 minutes. was the piece with the giant pinecone sliding and rubbing over an electrified kettle drum – just one of some 20 devices employed by percussionist William Winant. This was the soundscape “Duo Improvisation,” where seeing the players became as engrossing as listening. Chacon was on his multi-sound electric guitar, manipulating pedal controls as much as strumming. Meantime percussionist/showman Winant dove into a variety of instruments, working the drums of a stage set and churning about his Composer Raven Chacon won the 2022 Pulitzer Prize in Music. musical arsenal, ranging from shimmers of scrapes over his giant tam-tam to the high-pitched squeaks of a cymbal drawn across an electrified kettle. The pinecone journeyed across the drumskin and reached the far side, all the sounds enharmonic. This must-see duo ended in 20 minutes. The casual informality of the event offered a lot of fiddling – fiddling with the equipment and controls, that is. The conviviality at the break was welcome. This being Mills College, musicians and patrons milled about. When Chacon came over with all his luxurious saltand-pepper hair over the shoulders, people took photos of the celebrity. He is currently composer-in-residence at Mills and a star in an exotic musical medium. Exiting, I hoped that the lacrosse player was still doing his unmetered shots in his competing “concert.” But no, darkness had swept over the campus, and the sycamores untouched by the recent stormy blow stood inordinately quiet, perhaps out of respect. Perhaps because a relative, a pine tree, had provided a vital instrument for an epic concert experience. The Mills Center for Contemporary Music presentors have a distinguished history of bold sonic innovation. A half century ago this same hall had hosted internationally known experimental composers Pauline Oliveros, Lou Harrison, Karlheinz Stockhausen, John Cage, and Robert Ashley via the CCM. COMPOSER-IN-RESIDENCE RAVEN CHACON in his works March 18, Concert Hall, Mills College at Northeastern University, Oakland, CA. articles.text: David Morales conducts the choral group Cantare Con Vivo. Piedmonters know John Malick as an architect. They know Sue Malick as the leader of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Together they are master chemists – musically speaking. Anyone who attended the Sophie Florence Trio concert at the Center for the Arts on Friday evening observed the results of the Malicks’ musical chemistry. It seems that they were vacationing in Mexico and two of John’s friends were in the area at the same time. Being musicians, they brought their instruments. A young woman heard them jamming and asked to sing a song with them. The results sounded promising. So promising, that Sue Malick offered to sponsor them in a concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts this spring. The result? The Sophie Florence Trio made its debut in Piedmont on Friday, March 17. Everything looked promising. The audience was far flung – some even came from England. That’s the allure of music. But the chemistry needs to be right, and on Friday it was – from the opening notes. A sentimental ballad, “The House of the Rising Sun“, drew us in immediately. The music was enchanting. And wonder of wonders, the group knew how to add just the right amount of talking to go with the music. Sophie Florence has a gentle voice and she uses intimacy to best advantage. Backing her to perfection were Chuck Jacob on both the harmonica and string bass, and Phil Hirschi on guitar. Whether you call it alchemy or The Sophie Florence Trio performed a debut concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, March 17.

Cantare Con Vivo Two days later, another master musician produced alchemy of a different sort. David Morales has an enviable reputation. He is an inspired educator of young people and is Music Director of the well-established Cantare Con Vivo. Their musical vehicle on Sunday at the Scottish Rite Center, Oakland was a slight departure from the usual repertoire. It was Er nest Bloch’s intensely profound Sacred Service. Bloch was born in Switzerland but found success in the Bay Area. He was an instructor at UC Berkeley and also the Director of the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. In many ways Sacred Service is Bloch’s grandest composition. Its position in the Jewish musical liturgy is roughly the same as a high mass to Christians. What Bach did for the Christian liturgy Bloch did for the Jewish liturgy. The similarities are obvious. But the heartbreak is very different. Bach uses his music like a canvas painted by Velasquez. Bloch’s music is more like Picasso at Guernica. The performance of the Sacred Service featured baritone Simon Barrad, who was very convincing as the Cantor. Cantare Con Vivo sang up to their usual high-level. Everything was directed by the inspired leadership of Morales. It is interesting to note that good musicianship embraces all of humanity, and that’s how it was on Sunday. David Morales conducts the choral group Cantare Con Vivo. articles.text: The Secret Lives of Bees, is a family friendly, coming-of-age film based on the best-selling novel by Sue Monk, and is an ideal choice for tweens and newbie teens. It is set in North Carolina, the year is 1964, and has at its center a 14-year-old girl, Lily Owens (Dakota Fanning). Her mother is deceased and she is living with her abusive father, T.Ray (Paul Bettany), and a devoted housekeeper, Rosaleen (Jennifer Hudson). On a beautiful day, Rosaleen tells Lily that she wants to walk into town where she wants to register to vote; instead, she is attacked by a group of thuggish white racists. As a result Lily convinces Rosaleen that they need to escape the cruelty that confronts them daily and so they head for a nearby town call Tiburon. As always, Lily yearns to know the path her mother took just prior to her death. Through a series of serendipitous events, Lily and Rosaleen are taken in by a trio of sisters who live just outside of town where they keep hives of bees and make astonishingly good honey, sold by the local grocers. One owner of a local market tells Lily how to get to the source of the honey. Look for a pinkish two-story house, home of the Boatwrights. And indeed, when the two walk down a long dusty road, they do arrive at a garish home where they first meet August Boatwright (Queen Queen Latifah, Jennifer Hudson and Alicia Keys in a scene from The Secret Lives of Bees Latifah), the bee-keeping matriarch of the family, as well as the fiercely independent June (Alicia Key), a musician, and May (Sophie Okonedo), a tender-hearted, simple girl. Secret Lives evolves into a warm, generous story where Lily and Rosaleen are embraced by this extraordinary family, and Lily is introduced by August to the hives and comes to understand not only the meaning of family but the magic of making honey. There is also a bit of romance between Lily and a shy black teenager, Zach Taylor (Tristan Wilus), who make the mistake of going to town to see a movie. Innocently, they sit together in the theater. Though it is 1964, racism still survives, which the couple painfully learn is forbidden, and Zach is roughly arrested. The Secret Lives of Bees is never cloying, or overly sentimental. Nor is it a harsh southern documentary about prejudice and discrimination. Rather, it is a tale of strong black women created by a wonderful ensemble cast that will capture the audience from the first scene. The Secret Lives of Bees, Directed by Gina Prince-Bytherwood, Starring Queen Latifah, Jennifer Hudson, Alicia Keys. 1 hr., 50 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2008. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

By Chris Honoré The Secret Lives of Bees, is a family friendly, coming-of-age film based on the best-selling novel by Sue Monk, and is an ideal choice for tweens and newbie teens. It is set in North Carolina, the year is 1964, and has at its center a 14-year-old girl, Lily Owens (Dakota Fanning). Her mother is deceased and she is living with her abusive father, T.Ray (Paul Bettany), and a devoted housekeeper, Rosaleen (Jennifer Hudson). On a beautiful day, Rosaleen tells Lily that she wants to walk into town where she wants to register to vote; instead, she is attacked by a group of thuggish white racists. As a result Lily convinces Rosaleen that they need to escape the cruelty that confronts them daily and so they head for a nearby town call Tiburon. As always, Lily yearns to know the path her mother took just prior to her death. Through a series of serendipitous events, Lily and Rosaleen are taken in by a trio of sisters who live just outside of town where they keep hives of bees and make astonishingly good honey, sold by the local grocers. One owner of a local market tells Lily how to get to the source of the honey. Look for a pinkish two-story house, home of the Boatwrights. And indeed, when the two walk down a long dusty road, they do arrive at a garish home where they first meet August Boatwright (Queen Queen Latifah, Jennifer Hudson and Alicia Keys in a scene from The Secret Lives of Bees Latifah), the bee-keeping matriarch of the family, as well as the fiercely independent June (Alicia Key), a musician, and May (Sophie Okonedo), a tender-hearted, simple girl. Secret Lives evolves into a warm, generous story where Lily and Rosaleen are embraced by this extraordinary family, and Lily is introduced by August to the hives and comes to understand not only the meaning of family but the magic of making honey. There is also a bit of romance between Lily and a shy black teenager, Zach Taylor (Tristan Wilus), who make the mistake of going to town to see a movie. Innocently, they sit together in the theater. Though it is 1964, racism still survives, which the couple painfully learn is forbidden, and Zach is roughly arrested. The Secret Lives of Bees is never cloying, or overly sentimental. Nor is it a harsh southern documentary about prejudice and discrimination. Rather, it is a tale of strong black women created by a wonderful ensemble cast that will capture the audience from the first scene. articles.text: At a military ceremony with full flourishes on Wednesday, March 1, the Vandenburg Space Force Base Leadership School was renamed in honor of Chief Master Sergeant Arthur Hicks (1922-2017). His daughter Joyce Hicks, a Piedmont resident since 1987, spoke with the Piedmont Post on Thursday, March 9, about the legacy of her father’s life and career in the Air Force. “My dad felt his upward mobility was stunted because he was so outspoken about civil rights as a young officer,” Joyce said. He retired at Vandenberg after 28 years of military service in bases across the country, from Alaska to Tennessee. Having grown up poor as one of nine children in Atlanta, Georgia, Arthur joined the Army as a mechanic’s assistant in 1940 when he was 19. After seeing an ad in the local Post Office, he applied for and was hired by the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, now Tuskegee University. As World War II continued, the Army Air Corps, then segregated, needed more pilots so Arthur joined the Civilian Pilot Corps as a Cadet. Soon after, he became a commissioned officer. He became part of the Tuskegee Airmen, the first African-American military airmen in the U.S. Armed Forces, during World War II. “The war ended before he saw time overseas,” said Joyce, “and the Army then had no more need for so many pilots, so he was honorably discharged.” After the war, Arthur married Edith, and they Photo by Airman 1st Class Kadielle Shaw U.S. Space Force Col. Rob Long and Joyce Hicks, daughter of Arthur Hicks, cut the ribbon at the renaming ceremony of the Airman Leadership School at Vandenberg Space Force Base on March 1. had their first son in 1947. He then returned to the army through a program where honorably discharged officers could return as enlisted employees with the rank of Master Sergeant, the highest rank for enlisted men. In his new role as a Maintenance Supervisor for bomber aircraft, Arthur was stationed in Lockbourne, Ohio; then in Smyrna, Tennessee, and then four years at Elmendorf Air Force Base in Anchorage, Alaska, where Joyce was born in 1952. From Anchorage, the Hicks family was transferred to Lincoln, Nebraska, and then to Wichita Falls, Texas. Throughout these moves, Joyce said, her father continually “confronted racism in the military, and always spoke out against it.” In Wichita Falls, the base had Joyce attend a public school far away, instead of a segregated school five blocks from their house. This was in 1963, well after the 1952 Supreme Court case of Brown v. Board of Education which began the desegregation of U.S. public schools. “My father said that if I had to go to the school farther away, they had to send a driver. They did that for a week. After that, the base officials said, ‘Master Sergeant Hicks, your daughter can attend school in the neighborhood’,” Joyce said. From Texas, the family moved in 1963 to Vandenberg Air Force Base in California. But there, too, Arthur encountered trouble: on-base family housing was limited and nearby off-base housing for African-Americans was nonexistent. Through his persistence, he was soon promoted to Senior Master Sergeant, and then to Chief Master Sergeant, the highest enlisted rank in the Air Force and Space Force. After serving for 28 years, Arthur retired in 1970. He earned a Bachelor’s degree that year from the University of Nebraska, and then began a career of 13 years as a history and social studies teacher at Cabrillo High School in Lompoc, California, retiring in 1984. During this period, he also earned a Master’s degree from Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo. “I’m so proud that the [Vandenberg school] was named after him,” said Joyce. “He was a tireless worker, a leader who led by example. He and my mother encouraged me to be the best that I could be, and to exercise my advocacy skills by becoming a lawyer.” Joyce graduated from Berkeley Law School in 1977. She has worked as Chief Assistant to the City Attorney of Oakland, head of the Citizens Police Review Board in Oakland, and Director of the Department of Police Accountability in San Francisco. At the Vandenberg ceremony on March 1, she said: “My father’s advice was, ‘Find it in yourself to contribute to the whole. We can most effectively do that by first making the best possible contribution to our own selves; through education, through questioning, through personal growth and to look toward the goal that is so far out of reach you cannot even imagine what it is at this point in your life.’” GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2023 GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2023 GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2023 GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2023

articles.text: Registration for the free, 19th annual Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Features Showcase is now open. There will be two days of online tours on Saturday and Sunday, April 15-16, and two days of in-person tours on Saturday and Sunday, May 6-7. What’s special about California native plants? They are adapted to our soil and climate, naturally water conserving, and easy to care for. California native plants are better than non-native plants when it comes to attracting native birds, butterflies, and other forms of wildlife. As the gardens on the tour show, these lovely gardens display a sense of place that is uniquely Californian. The tours will also showcase green home features. Online tour The online Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Showcase will take place on April 15-16 from 10 a.m.-3 p.m. This event will be kicked off on April 15 with a keynote presentation by New York Times bestselling nature writer Doug Tallamy. The online tour will feature beautiful native plant gardens that attract birds, bees, and butterflies, as well as visits to homes with solar panels and backup batteries, heat pumps for heating and cooling the house and heating water, and induction ranges. In-person tour The in-person Natives Garden Tour will allow registrants to visit more than 50 beautiful, water-conserving native plant gardens in Alameda and Contra Costa counties on May 6-7 from 10 a.m.-5 p.m. All of the homes have native plant gardens; twenty will be sharing their green home features, such as solar panels and batteries, induction ranges, and heat pumps. Registrants will learn how to design a native plant garden for color and interest throughout the year, garden for wildlife, lower their water bills, protect their family’s health and the environment by gardening without using pesticides, and answering questions about electrification. How to register Register for the tours or learn more at BringingBacktheNatives. net. articles.text: Advanced Dentistry comes to Piedmont For the past 40 years, Dr. Daniel J Cobb provided innovative, high-quality dental care with friendly and comforting customer service. Dr. Cobb was renowned in the Bay Area for his extensive knowledge in implant dentistry and beloved for his kind demeanor. In June 2022, Piedmont lost a fixture of the community when Dr. Cobb passed suddenly from cancer. His loyal supporters are now witnessing a rebirth of the dental practice at the same location. Dr. Raion “Ryan” Sabo joins the Piedmont community with enthusiasm and passion for providing dental care at the highest quality. He developed his love for Piedmont during his undergraduate studies at UC Berkeley. After receiving his DDS degree from UC San Francisco, Dr. Sabo left the Bay Area to complete a 3-year residency program in Advanced Prosthodontics and became a specialist in complex aesthetic dentistry. When the opportunity to return to the East Bay and carry on Dr. Cobb’s legacy presented itself, a dream became a reality. “Piedmont provides the same tight-knit sense of community and small town vibes of my hometown of South Lake Tahoe, but simultaneously provides access to the amazing amenities Dr. Sabo and his staff occupy the former location of Dr. Daniel Cobb. of a large city. During our office remodel, my family, team, and I have already become frequent visitors of local Piedmont favorites: Ace Hardware, Neecha Thai, and Fenton’s Creamery”. Dr. Sabo is excited to continue exploring the area and start giving back to the community through both dentistry and various community outreach programs. The Piedmont Advanced Dentistry team wholeheartedly believes that despite the rapid rise of large corporate dental offices, there should always be a place to go for exceptional customer service, high-quality dental care, and a personal connection that takes the dental care experience to another level. This bespoke approach to dentistry is what Dr. Sabo strives to bring to Piedmont with his newly remodeled and rejuvenated dental practice. His goal is to make everyone who visits the office realize that dentistry can and should be a pleasant experience. All it takes is a skilled team of people who share a vision for excellence in quality care and kindness. Piedmont Advanced Dentistry is now accepting new patients Monday-Thursday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. and available for emergencies by appointment Friday to Sunday. The office accepts most major PPO dental insurance plans and offers their own in-office membership plan to help make high-quality dental care more affordable and accessible to everyone. articles.text: Dear Jim: I have a sump pump in my basement that has been doing its job fine for the last 10 years. When the big rains started in January, it failed, flooding the entire space and ruining my hardwood floors, rugs, and damaging the baseboards and sheetrock. It was an expensive nightmare. Why did this happen, and how do I keep this from happening again moving forward? Sump pumps can be used in a variety of ways to keep basements from flooding, either as stand-alone units inside a basement or crawlspace, or outside the house as part of a perimeter drainage system for below grade basements. While the pumps themselves are generally reliable and can often run 20-30 years without issues, it is primarily external factors that lead to their failure which can be minimized if the systems are monitored. Common causes of failure You need to check your pump at least twice a year and make sure it is plugged in and running, is in a clean basin not filled with dirt or debris, and with a float that moves up and down freely. The pump should be big enough to do the job, with a ¾ horsepower motor if water needs to go uphill to the street. A check valve needs to be installed next to the pump to keep water from running back into the pit or it may run continuously or way too often. The most common problem is with the GFI outlet that they are normally plugged into. Lack of a proper waterproof cover can allow moisture into the outlet, causing it to fail, especially when it is outside. If the pump is not running for an extended period due to a failed outlet and it remains submerged it can rust out and no longer function. If this sounds like Greek to you, find somebody who will review this information. Lack of attention and simple maintenance can have major consequences for finished basements. Backup systems can be a lifesaver The lesson we learned this year from looking at many of these failures is that things can go wrong in a heartbeat. In an atmospheric river downpour a basement can fill up with sevExamples of smart pumps and water-powered pumps A proper waterproof cover will protect this outlet. eral inches of water in 30 minutes or less, often when you are not around. Given that 100-year floods are something we may be getting every few years now, we are installing mandatory backup systems with our drainage work, such as dual pumps with battery backups, inverters to run main pumps from battery power, and our new favorite, the water-based pump that does not require electricity. We even have backups that tie into the internet and will send you alerts and real-time monitoring to your phone. Given that mother nature has a poor sense of humor and will likely cause this to happen while you are out of the country on winter break. this may be something for you to consider if you have an existing system that may be at risk. pages.text: Wednesday, March 22, 2023 23 Have you built an emergency fund? Many people make financial New Year’s resolutions, such as reducing their debts or contributing more to their retirement accounts — both of which are certainly worthy goals. But among those who planned to make a financial resolution for 2023, the primary reason was the desire to build an emergency savings fund, according to a December 2022 study by research firm Morning Consult. Factors such as economic concerns and the sharp rise in inflation seem to be driving this greater interest in building an emergency fund. But it’s extremely valuable to maintain this type of fund in any economic environment. An emergency fund can help you prepare for a temporary job loss or early retirement, or pay for large home or auto repairs, sizable medical bills and other needs. So, how much do you need to keep in an emergency fund? The answer depends on your stage of life. If you’re still working, you might want at least three to six months’ worth of living expenses in your emergency fund. If you’re already retired, however, you may need at least three months’ worth of expenses for emergencies, plus another 12 months’ worth of expenses, after accounting for your other sources of income, to cover your everyday spending needs. And if you are retired, it’s especially important to maintain this larger emergency fund so you can avoid dipping into your investment portfolio to pay for any unforeseen costs and daily expenses. As you know, the financial markets can be volatile, so, if it’s possible, you’ll want to avoid having to sell investments when their prices may be down. When building an emergency fund, where should you keep the money? You’ll need it to be accessible, so you’ll want it in a liquid investment vehicle. At the same time, you don’t want to take risks with this fund, so you’ll want to be confident that your principal will likely be preserved. Some possibilities might include short-term certificates of deposit (CDs) or money market accounts. But wherever you put the money, keep it separate from your regular checking or savings account — it’s called an “emergency” fund for a reason, and you don’t want to mingle it with the accounts you use every day. Given the high cost of living, it’s not always easy to sock away money for emergencies — and if you wait until all your bills are paid before addressing an emergency fund, you may only make very slow progress. One possible strategy is to pay yourself first, so to speak, by having some money automatically moved from your checking or savings account each month into your emergency fund. And whenever you get a financial windfall, such as a tax refund or a year-end bonus at work, you might use some of it for this fund. It will take time and discipline to build and maintain an emergency fund. But once you’ve got such a fund in place, you’ll feel more confident in your ability to deal with unexpected costs that could potentially disrupt your progress toward your financial goals. So, make it a priority this year to build or strengthen your emergency fund. It will be worth the effort. articles.text: Explaining Net Energy Metering After years of intense debate, the California Public Utility Commission (“CPUC”) voted unanimously on December 15 to overhaul the rules that govern the way homeowners and businesses are compensated for rooftop solar. The new set of rules, called Net Energy Metering 3.0 (NEM 3.0) will significantly reduce the amount that homeowners will be compensated for energy that is sent back into the power grid from their home solar systems. This change, which will take effect on April 15, 2023, may reduce the benefits of a new solar installation by as much as 75%. The most alarming impact will be the change in the export rate. The export rate is the rate that solar owners can “sell” their excess electricity back to the grid. Currently, solar owners can send energy back to the grid and receive credits EQUAL to the amount that PG&E sells consumers this electricity. Under NEM 3.0, PG&E will charge the consumer approximately 4x what they will credit back to residential solar owners for exporting their electricity (Export rates can vary widely, but studies show it will likely average about a 75% decrease). Clean energy advocates claim that the new rules will devastate the rooftop solar industry and set back progress in the state, while the utilities claim that the new rules do not go far enough to make solar owners pay their fair share for grid maintenance. Under NEM 3.0, the financial benefits of solar will be drastically diminished: • For buyers who pay cash for their Solar, payback “Breakeven” periods will increase. Currently payback periods are approximately 5-6 years and under the new regulation, this will jump closer to 9-10 years. • For buyers financing the systems, their monthly payments for energy will still generally be less than they were without solar. But savings will be 60% lower than current levels. • Complexity will be added to the Solar program by adding new requirements such as a new system design and a requirement to support self-storage. This being said, Consumers will still be able to save money going solar under NEM 3.0. Those who finance their system will still have savings if the system is properly designed and priced. Additionally, by being able to lock in the rate that you pay for electricity by owning solar, you can avoid having rapidly increasing energy bills. What does this mean for you? • Homeowners that DO NOT submit a Solar interconnection application prior to the April 15th deadline will be compensated for energy sent to the grid under the new regulatory rates. HOWEVER, Homeowners that submit prior to the April 15 deadline will be grandfathered into the current rate structure for 20 years, provided that the Solar installation is completed by April 14, 2026. Interconnection applications are prepared by a solar installer and require a signed contract and diagram to be submitted. • As we transition from fossil fuels to clean energy, a larger percentage of the energy we use in our homes and vehicles will be electric. In Piedmont, new Reach Codes will require homeowners making certain renovations to include energy efficiency or electrification measures. The Reach Codes also require some measures to prep homes for electrification, and even require installing solar in some cases. Given the April 15, 2023, deadline, we would encourage people who are considering Solar to reach out to installers to fully understand what solar and storage would look like for you under NEM 2.0 or NEM 3.0. To learn more, or see what these changes may mean to you, feel free to reach out to our team at quotes@bidlist.io. We can also recommend a lot of great solar companies in the area who can assist you. One answer lies in our kitchens and thinking more carefully about the food we buy, how it’s stored and cooked, and what we throw away. As US food production has streamlined and increased over the years, so, too, has food waste. Food waste and food scraps account for some 35 percent of what we throw away. A big bold, complex red, it possesses a dense ruby color along with a sweet nose of blueberries, currants and a touch or earth. Former Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King voiced her support of the adoption and shared her experience in developing the Element as a former City Council member. “I started working on the 6th Cycle Housing Element three years ago, back when former mayor Bob McBain was still in office,” King said. “This document is a result of government in action, of democracy in action, of hundreds and hundreds of conversations, communication, meetings, correspondence … and I really just want to cheer you on as you move this project forward.” The complete updated Housing Element and ancillary. articles.text: The Bond Oversight Committee reviewed city expenditures on the Community Pool Project at a meeting on Thursday, March 16. The review covered the period of December 5, 2022, when City Council approved a construction budget for Wickman Development & Construction, through February 28, 2023. Based upon a presentation by city Finance Director Michael Sczcech, the contract was awarded to the San Francisco-based Wickman for $21,700,000, with an overall construction budget of $23,870,000. Included in this is a $748,106 electrification fund, as City Council approved an all-electric pool design last April. The total Piedmont Community Pool budget is $28,981,000. The main costs which make this higher than the construction budget are a maximum of $2,550,694 provided to the firm ELS Architecture & Urban Design for engineering and design; $962,700 to Griffin Structures for project management; $36,990 to Isaac Sports Group for operational analysis; $16,956 to Rincon Consultants for a California Environmental Quality Act report; and $14,320 to the firm Forensic Analytical for environmental consulting. The primary source of funding for expenditures is Measure UU, which was approved by voters in November 2020. This measure authorized the city to issue up to $19.5 million in bonds, with revenue funding pool improvements. The revenue from these bonds is currently $24,556,809. The total budget for services covered by Measure UU, including construction, design, engineering, inspection, and management, is $24,718,577. All funding sources — including $3,054,177 in donations; $748,106 in loans and grants; and $460,140 in other funds available for the project — make the total budget $28,981,000. The city has spent $3,058,058 through February 28. A major amount of the donations have been generated by the non-profit Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO). As January, it had raised more than $1.25 million of its $2.1 million fundraising goal to bridge the gap presented by inflated construction costs since Measure UU was passed in late 2020. Since January, all donations to PRFO are being matched dollar for dollar up to $500,000 thanks to an anonymous donor. PRFO General Counsel Eric Havian noted that as of March 6, “we’ve received over half of the matching amount. I have a feeling we’re even closer now, and we hope to receive it all by June 1.” The pool project is still on-track to be completed by the summer of 2024.
